What this isAt a glanceWhat we fixedWhat we left outLimitationsWhat we checkedPhase plotsColumnsDownloads

What this is

Movement recorded from 12 participants: 488 recordings of 26 tasks, from walking, running and stairs to jumping, lifting and squatting. This is a local review version and is not released. The full version has 19,573 observations; the cleaned version has 19,448. An observation is one stride (8,831 in the full version), one movement span (10,254; each of 5,127 spans is exported once for the left and once for the right leg) or one whole recording (488). Strides and spans have exactly 150 samples from 0 to 100 percent; whole recordings keep their source sample times.

What we fixed and what we did not (original vs fixed)

One card per problem. Each card says what was wrong, how much of the source it touched, what we did, how it was checked, and what else it could affect. Example recordings were drawn at random with a recorded seed, not hand-picked. The earlier counts are source counts; the examples are from the source.

Mass and units

Per-kg moments and powers were divided by another participant's body mass

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. For 9 of 12 participants, the authors did not use the person's own body mass to turn moments and powers into per-kg values in level walking. For 7 of them the mass used is exactly another participant's listed body mass, and it can change between recordings of the same person.

How we know. The source gives some recordings in newton-metres as well as per kg. Dividing one by the other gives the mass that was used. Where that was not possible, the mass was estimated from force-plate moments.

What we did. We multiplied the moments and powers of 52 recordings by the mass the authors used divided by the person's own mass (factors from 0.70 to 1.59, median 1.04). For 7 of the 52 the mass used was worked out exactly; for 45 it is estimated from the force plates. The other 436 recordings stay as published with a note: 434 where the mass used cannot be told and 2 that are confirmed to use the person's own mass. Nothing was refit.

How it was checked. A second agent recomputed the list of 52 and every factor from the audit files and the publisher's mass table. In 12 randomly drawn recordings (7 rescaled, 5 kept) the rescaled columns equal the factor times the published values to 2e-16, and the kept recordings are identical to the source.

Example from the source. AB10, turn and step 1: the person's own mass is 67.5 kg, but force-plate moments point to about 83 kg being used. Published error against the person's own mass is 22 to 25%. This recording was drawn at random from the 45 shown recordings with a validated walking estimate.

How much of the source this touched, before the fix

52 of 488 recordings (10.7%) are shown to carry another mass; 15 more (3.1%) probably do; 2 are confirmed to use the person's own mass; 419 cannot be told. In level walking, 9 of 12 participants are affected.

Recordings are the source's 488 recordings from 12 participants. In level walking the affected per-kg values are 0.80 to 1.41 times the value for the person's own mass. Sample counts were not part of these checks.

What else this could affect

A wrong mass changes per-kg moments and powers. It does not change angles, forces or the pressure point.

  • Also wrong, fixed Hip, knee and ankle moments (per kg). In the 52 recordings they are now scaled to the person's own mass. How we know: Factor times published value, to 2e-16, in the 7 rescaled recordings that were drawn.
  • Also wrong, fixed Hip, knee and ankle powers (per kg). Power carries the same mass, so it got the same factor in the same recordings. How we know: The match between power and moment times speed is the same before and after the rescale (largest difference 1.6e-15 in slope).
  • Checked, not affected Joint angles and angle speeds. Mass divides only the moments, so angles do not change with it.
  • Checked, not affected Ground forces in newtons and the pressure point. They are not divided by this mass. How we know: Newton forces equal the plate columns exactly in all 488 recordings, so no mass is inside them.
  • Open limit The 45 estimated factors. They rest on force-plate estimates matched to the nearest listed mass: the remaining error is at most 11 percent (median 4 percent) if the mass used is a listed one. For two AB09 recordings the nearest listed mass is about 5 percent below the estimate. How we know: 45 recordings, 3,253 observations carry this note; the 2 AB09 recordings hold 128 of them.
  • Open limit Agreement with a local newton-metre re-run. A local re-run exists for 7 recordings. The rescaled values match it to 0.001 N·m in 3 of them, miss by 0.02 to 0.5 percent of the peak in 3, and one could not be lined up. A recording that was never rescaled misses by the same relative amount, so this is a limit of the re-run, not of the mass. How we know: 7 recordings, 1,817 observations carry this note.
  • Not checked Moments and powers in the 436 kept recordings. They are not shown to carry another mass; they are neither confirmed nor cleared.

The README says moments are in N·m and powers in W, but the data are per kg

Documented, not a data fix

What was wrong. The publisher's README lists joint moments in N·m and powers in W. The published values were already divided by body mass, so they are in N·m per kg and W per kg.

How we know. A moment rebuilt from the force plates in N·m is 64 to 90 times larger than the published ankle moment, which is a body mass. Joint power equals the published moment times joint speed (ratio 0.96 to 1.00).

What we did. Documented only. In this version the moment and power columns are named per kg (newton-metres per kg and watts per kg), the unit is recorded with every column, and nothing is divided by mass a second time.

Example from the source. AB01, incline walking 2, left leg: read as N·m, the published ankle moment is 1/64 to 1/90 of the force-plate moment, in all 8 sampled legs (98 to 99% too small).

How much of the source this touched, before the fix

All 488 recordings (100%) carry the README's wrong unit text. The check measured 5 participants (25 channel files, 8 legs) and found the same result in all.

The README applies to every recording. The units check itself sampled 5 of 12 participants; the other 7 are covered by the README text only. Sample counts do not apply.

What else this could affect

Wrong unit text would make every moment and power 64 to 90 times too small for anyone who trusts it. Angles and forces are not in these units.

  • Checked, not affected Moments (per kg). LocoHub labels them N·m per kg and does not divide again. How we know: Both current converters copy the values as per kg.
  • Checked, not affected Powers (per kg). Labelled W per kg for the same reason. How we know: Power equals moment times joint speed, ratio 0.96 to 1.00 in the checked legs.
  • Checked, not affected Ground forces. The unit text does not touch forces. How we know: Force-plate body mass matches the README mass in 5 of 5 checked participants.
  • Not checked The authors' filtered and processed moment and power files. Only 3 recordings were compared with the raw moments and they match; the filtered and power files were not compared.

Forces in body weights use the wrong mass for AB03

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. Both converters take the body mass for body-weight forces from a local table that was rewritten from the body models. For AB03 it says 82.18 kg, but the publisher's table and the force plates say about 113.5 kg. The other participants in the table differ by rounding only (below 0.1%).

How we know. The publisher's mass table and the local table were compared. In the force-plate check, AB03's body mass came out near 114 kg, not 82.

What we did. Forces in body weights for all 40 AB03 recordings now use the publisher's mass of 113.5 kg. The local table's 82.18 kg is never read. Every other participant uses the publisher's table mass.

How it was checked. In AB03's standing recording the total vertical force has a median of 1.004 body weights, which implies 113.9 kg; the old 82.18 kg would give 1.39. In 14 randomly drawn recordings the body-weight columns equal the newton columns divided by mass times gravity exactly.

Example from the source. AB03 forces divided by 82.18 kg instead of 113.5 kg come out 1.38 times too large in body weights.

Forces and pressure point

Horizontal ground force is labelled forward and sideways, but is in lab axes

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The converters write the force plates' horizontal force in lab directions straight into the forward and sideways columns. Lab directions turn with the person, so they are not forward and sideways unless the person walks along one lab axis.

How we know. The paper says the forces are in the lab frame. The converter code copies them without turning them by the person's facing direction.

What we did. Every recording now carries the horizontal force in lab axes under lab-axis names, in newtons and body weights. The forward and sideways columns are filled only in the 11 forward-walking tasks, turned by the facing direction measured from the pelvis markers, and left empty in the other 15 tasks.

How it was checked. A second implementation reproduced the angles, the pressure point and the force columns of the conversion step, and a separate readback compared every exported observation with its inputs (largest difference 2.0e-9 on forces of about a thousand newtons).

Example from the source. Walking in a straight line can keep one lab axis nearly fixed, so the error can hide there; a turn or a side shuffle shows it at once.

398 of 488 recordings (81.6%) have event windows and would be exported with the wrong labels; the other 90 are never exported by either converter.

Recordings in the source (488). Samples were not counted: nothing was converted for this review.

In this version. In this version all 488 recordings are exported, not only the 398 that had event windows.

What else this could affect

A wrong force direction changes the forward and sideways force and anything computed from it, such as braking and push-off. It does not change up-down force, angles, or the moments the authors published.

  • Also wrong, fixed Forward and sideways force. No longer lab-axis values under forward and sideways names: they are filled only where the person walks forward, and lab-axis values keep their own names.
  • Checked, not affected Up-down force. Up is a lab axis and positive means support.
  • Checked, not affected Published moments and powers. The authors computed them in the lab frame, so the labelling does not change them.
  • Open limit Facing direction inside a stride. The person's heading is not constant inside a stride: the median of the largest heading deviation per stride is about 6° and the largest is about 18 to 23°.
  • Not checked Forces and heading. No coarse limit exists for them, so the structured assessment did not check them.

Some tasks have no single forward direction

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. Our rule says forward means the walking direction. In 15 of the 26 tasks the person does not walk forward in one direction: backward walking, side shuffle, squats, sit-to-stand, lifting, jumps, lunges, turns, cutting and meandering.

How we know. The authors' task descriptions were read, and the heading of the pelvis during each window was reviewed; only the 11 forward-walking tasks have a steady heading that matches the direction of travel.

What we did. As decided, forward and sideways force and pressure point are filled only for the 11 forward-walking tasks. The other 15 tasks keep lab-axis values only; their forward and sideways columns are empty.

How it was checked. The empty columns and their reasons are listed per observation, and a separate readback checked that exactly the missing columns are listed as empty.

Example from the source. One of the 15, drawn at random: twister. Its horizontal force stays in lab axes.

15 of 26 tasks (57.7%) and 241 of 488 recordings (49.4%) keep lab-axis horizontal force and pressure point only.

This decision changes only the forward and sideways force and pressure point. Up-down force and angles are not touched.

  • Left out Forward and sideways force in the 15 tasks. Empty; the lab-axis values are kept under lab-axis names.

  • Not checked Forward walking: stairs and curbs. The checks of braking, push-off and pressure-point progression gave no answer on stairs, so the facing direction there is not confirmed.

The pressure point's origin is the heel bone, not a point 100 mm forward of the ankle centre

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The converters give the centre of pressure (where the force acts on the foot) in a frame attached to the heel bone, which turns with the foot. The origin is the heel-bone frame origin, not the ankle as a code comment says. LocoHub's data reference now says the frame turns with the foot and its origin is 100 mm forward of the ankle joint centre along the heel-to-toe direction.

How we know. The calculation was read: the pressure point in the lab is turned into the foot frame using the foot's position and orientation, with no ankle offset.

What we did. The pressure point is now given in the ankle frame, which turns with the foot, inside that leg's side-view plane. Its origin is 100 mm forward of the ankle joint centre along the foot direction. Forward is along the foot, up is perpendicular to it in the plane, and sideways is out of the plane, so toe-out shows as a sideways offset. For step-ups and curb-ups the pressure point is left empty, because the foot is on a raised surface of unknown height.

How it was checked. A second implementation reproduced the pressure point to 2e-16 m. The rule was applied to the written values in a separate readback of every observation.

Example from the source. Moving the origin from the heel-bone frame origin to a point 100 mm forward of the ankle centre shifts every forward and up value by a fixed amount in the foot frame. The size of that shift was not measured.

How much of the source this touched, before the fix

398 of 488 recordings (81.6%) have a pressure point in the foot frame; the other 90 are never exported.

Recordings in the source (488). Samples were not counted.

In this version. In this version all 488 recordings are exported. The pressure point is empty where a plate was not loaded, a marker was missing, or the foot stood on a raised surface; each case has a stated reason.

An origin error shifts every pressure-point value by a fixed amount in the foot frame, and affects anything computed from it, such as moments about the ankle or how the pressure point moves along the foot. It does not change the force itself.

  • Also wrong, fixed Forward, up and sideways pressure point. Now in the ankle frame with its origin 100 mm forward of the ankle joint centre.

Curb-ups: the heel is 0.20 to 0.23 m above the recorded plate surface (268 observations in 12 recordings). Force and the plate's own pressure point stay.

Joint signs and angles

The source's knee sign is opposite to LocoHub's

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The authors' plotting code and paper show hip and knee in the extension-positive direction for the segmented data, and the ankle in the dorsiflexion-positive direction. LocoHub's rule needs flexion positive for hip and knee. The knee therefore needs its sign flipped, in angle, speed and moment; hip and ankle stay as they are.

How we know. The authors' plotting code was read for its sign changes and the paper's description of the plots. The sign detector was then run on 3 participants.

What we did. Knee angle, knee speed and knee moment now follow LocoHub's rule (flexion positive). The angles come from our own segment angles, the speeds are recomputed from them, and the knee moment is the published knee moment times −1. Power keeps its sign. Hip and ankle moments are as published.

How it was checked. A separate readback of every exported observation checks that the knee moment is the negated published value; it fails if a knee moment is not negated.

Example from the source. AB01, AB06 and AB13 were checked on level, incline, decline and stair walking: the detector gave a sign for 141 of 180 channel checks and none was wrong; for 39 it gave no answer.

How much of the source this touched, before the fix

All 488 recordings (100%) need the knee flip. 20 recordings (4.1%) were checked on real data: 141 of 180 channel checks right, 0 wrong, 39 no answer.

Recordings in the source (488). The checks counted 20 recordings and 180 channel checks (hip, knee and ankle angle, moment and power). Samples were not counted.

In this version. The sign evidence from the source (20 recordings, 141 of 180 channel checks right, 0 wrong, 39 no answer) is unchanged and still covers walking, inclines, declines and stairs in 3 participants only.

Pelvis, thigh and shank angles are not in the source

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The publisher gives joint angles (hip, knee, ankle) but no pelvis, thigh or shank angles. The local files that have them were made by our own earlier processing (a fixed turn order with a quarter-turn offset for the pelvis), which is not the publisher's definition.

How we know. All 7,038 entries in the publisher's archive were searched and none holds segment angles or segment speeds.

What we did. We computed pelvis, thigh, shank and foot angles ourselves, as angles measured against gravity. The pelvis is measured in its own plane from the hip-bone markers; each leg is measured in the vertical plane perpendicular to its knee axis, found from the knee markers. Thigh and shank directions come from the authors' scaled body model, the foot from heel and toe markers. Hip, knee and ankle angles are the differences of these. Joint speeds are recomputed from the angles by central difference, without smoothing.

How it was checked. A second implementation reproduced the angles to 9e-16 radians. All 488 recordings were scanned for a one-sample jump of more than 90°: only AB13 dynamic walk 1 has one (one whole turn on the right foot and ankle), and it was unwrapped.

Example from the source. Pelvis tilt for AB02's level walking could be computed from the local transform tables. Its sign and zero are now set by the data reference; no source value exists to check it against.

The README and the paper describe joint speed differently

Documented, not a data fix

What was wrong. The README says joint speed is a one-step backward difference of the angle. The paper says the angles were filtered and differentiated with a centred difference. Both cannot be right.

How we know. The README text, the paper's methods and the authors' code were compared.

What we did. Not a data fix. The publisher's speeds are not stored. The joint speeds in this version are recomputed from our angles by central difference at the source sample rate, without smoothing, so they do not depend on which description is right. Moments and powers are the publisher's values.

Example from the source. Which difference was used decides how smooth the speed looks near fast changes, such as heel strike.

Events and task labels

Running and skipping files are labelled as level walking

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. LocoHub's converter labels every normal-walk file as level walking. The authors group the 2.0 and 2.5 m/s files as running and the skipping files as skipping.

How we know. The authors' grouping code, their plotting script and the paper's Table 1 all call the 2.0 and 2.5 m/s files running.

What we did. Task labels follow the authors' grouping. The 2.0 and 2.5 m/s cycles are labelled run (795 cycles in 9 recordings) and the skipping cycles are labelled skip (134 cycles). Shuffle cycles stay under level walking with their own task name (115 cycles in 11 recordings). Walking cycles with no speed or slope label are filed under functional task rather than guessed (2,463 cycles in 36 recordings). The source task name is kept with every observation.

How it was checked. The label rules were checked against the README text in a readback of all 19,573 observations. Of the 795 run cycles, 706 had force data for a flight check and all 706 show a flight phase (both feet off the plates).

Example from the source. AB05: 3 of its 7 normal-walk event files would be relabelled (running at 2.0 and 2.5 m/s, and skipping). AB05 was drawn at random.

33 of 77 event files (42.9%) carry the wrong task label: 22 running and 11 skipping. They come from 11 of 12 participants; 4 of the running files hold no events.

The unit is event files (the authors' start and end times, one file per condition and recording): 77 normal-walk files in 12 recordings. Windows and samples were not counted per file.

The phase export drops the second leg's steps

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. For each task the phase converter keeps only the leg with more event windows and drops the other leg's. The dropped windows include running and stairs steps and hop contacts.

How we know. The converter code was read and the kept and dropped counts were recomputed from the authors' event files, task by task.

What we did. We cut the strides and movement spans ourselves, for every leg. Gait strides carry the foot that makes them. Each movement span is exported once for the left and once for the right leg. 9,378 of the authors' 13,119 event windows are matched and exported; each of the other 3,741 has a stated reason in the left-out list.

How it was checked. Where a plate is loaded, our strides reproduce the authors' strides exactly in the gait tasks (start and end offset 0 ms): normal walk 1,590 of 1,595 windows, dynamic walk 747 of 749, incline walk 744 of 744, backward walk 572 of 572, weighted walk 166 of 166. A separate readback re-derived the counts.

Example from the source. lift weight, drawn at random from the tasks that lose windows: 570 windows dropped, 570 kept.

4,948 of 13,119 event windows (37.7%) never reach the phase export, in 15 of 26 tasks, which hold 343 of 488 recordings (70.3%). That includes 498 single-leg gait cycles (running and stairs) and 127 hop contacts.

The unit is event windows: 13,119 in all 787 event files of the source (7,721 left, 5,398 right). The grid counts recordings that have windows in tasks that lose some; the per-participant split of dropped windows was not read (it needs a guarded job). Samples were not counted.

In this version. This version has 8,831 strides, 10,254 span observations and 488 whole recordings.

The time export merges all of a file's events into one window

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The time-based converter makes one window per event file, from the earliest start to the latest end of every field in it. Files that hold several conditions (such as sitting and standing, or forward and backward) become one window that includes the time between them. The reference leg is simply the first start.

How we know. The converter code was read, and its window count was compared with the authors' counts.

What we did. No windows are merged. Each stride or movement span is its own observation with its own start and end in source time, and each recording appears once, whole, in the time file.

How it was checked. A separate readback found the exported set equal to the expected set in both directions, with no duplicate identities.

Example from the source. The source holds 13,119 event windows in 778 non-empty files; the converter writes 778 windows.

A backup segmentation could replace the source's events

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. When an event file lacks left and right fields, the phase converter replaces the source events with its own segmentation using fixed force thresholds (600 and 400 N). Any output made that way is not source-defined.

How we know. The converter code was read, and every sit-to-stand and jump event file was found to have source fields, so the backup should never run.

What we did. The old converters and their backup segmentation are not used. This version is built from our own source reader, our own segmentation and our own conventions, and each step's output is bound by hash to the checked output of the step before.

How it was checked. The hashes of every input were checked against the guarded-job receipts by a second agent.

Task details and source limits

The converter wrote stair, curb and step heights nobody measured

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The converter writes a stair height of 0.15 m (the paper says 152 mm), calls the pass number a step number, and writes 0.15 m for curbs and 0.20 m for step-ups. The curb and step-up heights are not in any local source.

How we know. The converter's task-detail code was compared with the paper's Table 1. The paper's supplementary protocol table is not available locally.

What we did. The stair rise is 0.152 m, citing the paper's Table 1. The pass number is named pass number. No curb or step-up height is written, because no source gives one. Speeds and inclines appear only where the authors' label or the README states them.

How it was checked. A separate readback of every observation checked the stair rise, the speeds and inclines, and that no curb or step height is present.

Example from the source. Stairs at 0.15 m instead of 0.152 m is 1.3% off; the curb and step-up heights are unchecked.

Nothing has been reconverted from the full source yet

Fixed and checked

What was wrong. The source holds 488 recordings, each with 10 channel files (4,880 in all, 39.1 GB uncompressed). No reviewed conversion of all of them exists, so every number on this page describes the source or the old converter code, not new output.

How we know. The local folders and the publisher archive were listed and matched recording by recording. This is a listing, not a check of any value.

What we did. All 488 recordings (4,880 channel files) were read and converted in guarded jobs run one at a time, with the code frozen after pilots. The full run covered 12 participants, passed 28 checks, peaked at 418 MiB and took 769 seconds. The result is the local review version on this page: 19,573 observations in the full version and 19,448 in the cleaned version, with every file hash checked by a second agent.

How it was checked. A second agent recomputed all file hashes, checked that the cleaned version is the full version minus 125 failures and nothing else, and compared a random sample of 10 observations with the source.

What we checked and what we did not

Checked

  • Every exported observation was read back by separate code and compared with its inputs: the largest difference is 2.0e-9, which is float precision on forces of about a thousand newtons.
  • All file hashes match; the cleaned version is the full version minus 125 failures and nothing else; every phase observation has exactly 150 samples from 0 to 100 percent, and the phase files pass the data contract with no issues.
  • Segment angles, joint angles and the pressure point were recomputed by a second implementation to 9e-16 radians and 2e-16 m.
  • Mass factors for 52 recordings and the 40 AB03 body-weight columns were recomputed independently.
  • Where a plate is loaded, our own strides reproduce the authors' strides exactly in the gait tasks.
  • Hip, knee and ankle angles against coarse limits (hip −50 to 150°, knee −30 to 165°, ankle −80 to 50°), angles for jumps of 30° or more between neighbouring samples, the pressure point against 0.5 m forward and 0.3 m up and sideways of the foot, and a left-right side check. 19,448 of 19,573 observations pass; 125 fail.
  • Every item left out of either version has a row and a reason in the left-out list: 5,281 rows.

Not checked

  • Joint speeds, moments, powers, ground forces, the lab-axis pressure point and heading have no limit, so they were not assessed. A missing or unassessed signal is not evidence of passing.
  • Where the ankle angle is zero has not been checked.
  • The limits themselves are a draft written before any of these data were read. They are not approved reference ranges.
  • The two time files were not run through the data contract.
  • Source files were checked against the job receipts, not hashed again from the source.
  • The 45 estimated mass factors are estimates; their truth was not checked.
  • The cause of the AB07 right-foot offset and of the AB03 side-shuffle plate mismatch is unresolved.
  • The forward-direction and force-plate height assumptions for right-plate treadmill recordings were not checked.

A passing check is not scientific approval. This page approves the conversion arithmetic and the file structure only.

Columns are listed for the stride files; the time files carry the same signals with left and right names instead of this-leg and other-leg names. A column can be empty in an observation where a plate or marker is missing; the reason is written in the file's list of empty signals.
